title: Japan Changes Tax-Free Shopping Rules for Tourists
paragraphs: Shopping in Japan has changed for foreign tourists.
Until recently, tourists could buy many products without paying Japan's consumption tax. This tax is 8% on food and nonalcoholic drinks, and 10% on most other products.
But since November 1, visitors have had to pay this tax when they buy things, even at tax-free shops.
However, they can get this money back at a later time.
When they're ready to leave Japan, they can complete a customs check to get back the tax they'd paid via credit card or another payment method.
Tourists can only claim refunds on products they take out of Japan themselves — and they must do so within 90 days of buying them.
However, the previous 500,000 yen ($3,200) spending limit on consumable products, such as food and cosmetics, has been removed.
The changes come after growing concerns that some tourists had been buying products tax-free and then reselling them within Japan.
As tourism in Japan has grown, tax-free shopping has become a much bigger business.
According to data from the Japan Tourism Agency, in 2025, foreign visitors spent around 9.5 trillion yen — or $60 billion — in Japan. This was almost three times as much as 10 years earlier.

And as tourists spend more, the amount of tax they don't have to pay has also become a topic of debate. In 2025, some Japanese politicians even considered ending tax-free shopping for tourists completely, after tax exemptions reached around 200 billion yen, or $1.2 billion, in 2024.
But Japanese retail groups disagreed. They argued that ending the system could make Japan less attractive to international visitors and hurt businesses that depend on tourist spending.
For now, tax-free shopping hasn't disappeared in Japan. Tourists can still save money — but they have to pay the tax first and claim it back later.
